task-item.what: A single to-do entry in a list, with a way to mark it done and a short description of what needs doing.
uses: Personal and team to-do lists.
Checklists for repeated processes such as onboarding or launches.
Project follow-up lists with owners and dates.
avoid: Complex work with many steps and dependencies: use a timeline or board instead.
Plain notes with nothing to complete: use text.
practices: Start the title with a verb so it reads as an action.
Let people tick a task off with one click.
Show owner and due date next to the title.
Keep titles short enough to fit on one line.

subtask-item.what: A smaller step that belongs to a larger task. It is usually shown indented beneath its parent.
uses: Breaking a big task into steps that can be finished one at a time.
Checklists inside a task, such as items to pack or review.
Letting several people each own a part of one task.
avoid: Steps that are really separate pieces of work: make them tasks of their own.
Deep nesting: more than two levels gets hard to read.
practices: Indent subtasks clearly under their parent.
Show how many subtasks are done on the parent.
Keep to one level of nesting.
Complete the parent only when all steps are done, or say why not.

milestone-item.what: A marker for an important point in a plan, such as a launch or approval, shown with its name, date and state.
uses: Roadmaps showing key dates.
Project overviews that track big checkpoints.
Reporting progress to people who do not need task detail.
avoid: Everyday work that takes time: use a task.
Hard external dates with legal or financial weight: use a deadline.
practices: Name milestones as outcomes, such as 'Pilot live'.
Show a clear date and a state in words.
Keep the list short so each one matters.
Mark missed milestones plainly, not only with colour.

deadline-item.what: An entry for a date by which something must be done, showing what is due and how much time is left or how late it is.
uses: Compliance and legal dates.
Renewals for licences, contracts or subscriptions.
Lists of what is due soon across several projects.
avoid: Soft targets in a plan: use a milestone.
Work that people tick off in a list: use a task.
practices: Show the exact date and the time remaining.
Make overdue items stand out with words as well as colour.
Sort the nearest deadline first.
Tell people what is due, not only that something is.

reminder-item.what: A prompt that reminds someone about something at a set time, with quick ways to act on it or put it off.
uses: Notification lists of things that have come due.
Follow-ups on tasks or appointments.
Sidebars that gather what needs attention today.
avoid: Messages that need a reply or a decision: use a message or task.
System errors and warnings: use an alert.
practices: State what the reminder is about in plain words.
Show when it was set for.
Offer snooze and done right on the item.
Let people choose how long to snooze.

assignee-chip.what: A small tag showing who is responsible for an item, usually a picture or initials with a name.
uses: Showing the owner of a task or ticket.
Cards on a board where people scan for their own work.
Filter lists by person.
avoid: Showing a group of many people: use an avatar stack with a count.
Long contact details: link to a profile instead.
practices: Show the person's name as well as their picture.
Show 'Unassigned' clearly when nobody owns the item.
Keep the chip the same size as other chips.
Make it clickable only if it does something useful.

due-date-chip.what: A small tag that shows the date something is due, and changes its look as the date gets close or passes.
uses: Tasks and cards that have a due date.
Lists where people sort or scan by date.
Warning that something is late.
avoid: Dates that are only informational, such as when something was created: use plain text.
Exact times of meetings: use an event.
practices: Use relative words such as 'Tomorrow' for dates close by.
Show the full date for dates further away.
Mark overdue items with a word, not only red.
Use the same date format everywhere.

status-chip.what: A small tag that says what state an item is in, such as planned, in progress, done or overdue.
uses: Showing progress of tasks, requests or runs.
Filtering lists by state.
Helping people see at a glance what needs attention.
avoid: Counts or percentages of progress: use a progress bar.
Urgent system problems: use an alert.
practices: Use a short word for every state, never colour alone.
Keep the same set of states across the product.
Give each state its own shape or icon.
Do not invent extra states unless people need them.

priority-chip.what: A small tag that shows how important or urgent an item is, such as low, medium, high or urgent.
uses: Ordering tasks and tickets by importance.
Helping teams decide what to work on first.
Filtering lists to the most urgent items.
avoid: Dates and deadlines: use a due date.
Too many levels: three or four are enough.
practices: Pair the symbol with a word so it works without colour.
Hide the normal level to reduce clutter.
Keep the scale small and the order obvious.
Use the same wording everywhere.

progress-chip.what: A small tag showing how much of an item is finished, with a tiny bar and a count such as 3/5.
uses: Tasks with subtasks or checklists.
Plans and projects shown in lists.
Letting people see progress without opening the item.
avoid: Long waits such as uploads: use a full progress bar.
Items with only one step: use a status.
practices: Show both the count and the bar.
Count finished steps out of the total.
Add a text label for screen readers.
Update it as soon as a step is done.

gantt-bar.what: A horizontal bar on a calendar-like grid, showing when a task starts and ends, and often how far along it is.
uses: Project timelines with tasks that overlap.
Roadmaps showing what happens when.
Spotting delays and gaps in a plan.
avoid: Simple to-do lists: use a task list.
Tracking work by stage: use a board.
practices: Show a clear time scale at the top.
Mark late and finished work in more than colour.
Offer a list version for screen readers.
Let the grid scroll sideways on small screens.

plan-card.what: A card that summarises one plan or project: its name, time period, how far along it is and what remains.
uses: Lists of projects, sprints or rollouts.
Dashboards showing several plans together.
Quickly spotting which plans are late.
avoid: Detailed plan content: open the plan page instead.
A single task: use a task item.
practices: Show the period and progress together.
Put the name first and make the whole card clickable.
Include counts of open, done and late items.
Keep every card the same shape.

board-card.what: A small card for one piece of work on a board of columns, such as a kanban board.
uses: Tracking work as it moves between stages.
Team task boards.
Sales or hiring pipelines.
avoid: Long text or lots of detail: link to a full page.
Work with strict date order: use a timeline.
practices: Show only the key facts: title, owner and date.
Keep every card the same layout.
Provide a menu to move cards without dragging.
Make the title a link to the full item.

resource-row.what: A row for one person, team or piece of equipment, showing how busy they are across days or weeks.
uses: Planning who can take on more work.
Staff rosters and shift schedules.
Booking shared equipment or rooms.
avoid: Individual task lists: use tasks.
Showing a single appointment: use a calendar event.
practices: Line up every row on the same days.
Show hours as numbers, not only colours.
Label each day cell for screen readers.
Show total load beside the name.

alert.what: A message that tells people something happened and needs their attention, such as an error, a warning or a success.
uses: Showing that an action failed and how to fix it.
Warnings about problems with the system or an account.
Results that should stay visible on the page.
avoid: Quick confirmations that can disappear: use a toast.
Permanent tips and notes: use a callout.
practices: Say what happened in the title and what to do in the text.
Use plain words, not codes.
Never rely on colour alone to show the type.
Do not show more than one or two at a time.

callout.what: A highlighted box that draws attention to a note, tip, warning or limit within the content of a page.
uses: Explaining a consequence before someone acts.
Tips and limits on settings pages.
Pointing out an important note inside documentation.
avoid: Results of something the user just did: use an alert.
Content that makes up most of the page: use normal text.
practices: Keep it to a sentence or two.
Use a clear title and an icon.
Pick the tone to match the message.
Use few callouts per page or they get ignored.

empty-state.what: What people see when a page or list has nothing to show yet, such as a new account or a search with no results.
uses: First use, before any content exists.
Searches or filters with no matches.
A cleared inbox or finished list.
avoid: Small areas such as one chart: use a short no-data message.
Loading in progress: use a loading indicator.
practices: Say why it is empty in plain words.
Offer the next step, such as a create button.
Keep a friendly, calm tone.
Suggest how to change the search when nothing matches.

no-data-state.what: A short message in a chart, table or tile that has nothing to show, saying there is no data and why.
uses: Charts with no data for the chosen dates.
Table bodies when filters match nothing.
Dashboard tiles that have not collected data yet.
avoid: Whole pages with nothing yet: use an empty state.
Content still loading: use a loading indicator.
practices: Say there is no data, and give the reason if known.
Keep the message the same size as what it replaces.
Do not leave charts or tables blank.
Tell people how to get data if they can.

status-light.what: A small coloured dot with a word showing whether something is working, such as online, offline or degraded.
uses: Showing whether a device or service is up.
Job or connection state in lists and headers.
Dashboards of many systems.
avoid: Progress of a task: use a progress bar.
Anything that needs explaining: use an alert.
practices: Always include a word, not only a colour.
Show since when the state has held.
Use the same state words everywhere.
Keep the dot small and consistent in size.

dialog.what: A window that opens on top of the page and asks people to finish a short task or make a choice before going on.
uses: Short tasks such as renaming or choosing an option.
Confirming a choice.
Collecting one or two details.
avoid: Long forms: use a separate page.
Content people need to compare with the page: use a side panel.
practices: Give it a clear title that names the task.
Move focus into the dialog and back when it closes.
Let Escape and a close button dismiss it.
Put the main action first and label it with a verb.

confirm-dialog.what: A dialog that asks people to confirm before something that cannot be undone, such as a deletion.
uses: Deleting data or accounts.
Cancelling a running process.
Removing someone's access.
avoid: Actions that can be reversed: do them and offer Undo.
Common, harmless actions: asking each time causes fatigue.
practices: Ask a question that names the thing affected.
Say what will happen in one sentence.
Label the button with the action, such as Delete video.
Put focus on the safe choice, Cancel.

progress-with-counts.what: A progress bar with a label and numbers saying how much is done, how much remains and how long it may take.
uses: Uploads, exports and imports.
Batch jobs that process many items.
Multi-step tasks that take more than a few seconds.
avoid: Waits under a second or two: no indicator is needed.
Unknown length: use a simple loading spinner.
practices: Show real numbers, such as 77 of 120.
Give a time estimate when it is reliable.
Tell people about failures as they happen.
Announce when it finishes.

toast.what: A small message that appears briefly, usually at the edge of the screen, to confirm something just happened.
uses: Confirming a saved or sent item.
Offering Undo after a quick action.
Short updates that need no reply.
avoid: Errors and warnings people must act on: use an alert.
Messages people must be able to read later: keep them on the page.
practices: Keep it to one short sentence.
Leave it up long enough to read, about 5 seconds.
Pause it while someone points at it.
Never move keyboard focus to it.

flash-message.what: A message shown at the top of the next page after a form is sent, telling people what the result was.
uses: Confirming a record was created, saved or deleted.
Reporting that a form submission failed.
Showing the result after a redirect.
avoid: Errors next to a form field: show them beside the field.
Instant feedback without leaving the page: use a toast.
practices: Place it where people will see it first.
State clearly what was done.
Let people dismiss it.
Use the right tone for success, warning and error.

tooltip.what: A small label that appears when someone hovers over or focuses on an item, to name or explain it.
uses: Naming icon-only buttons.
Showing the full text of a shortened label.
Giving a quick hint about a control.
avoid: Important information: put it on the page where everyone can see it.
Touch devices, where hover does not exist: show the label.
practices: Keep it to a few words.
Make it appear on keyboard focus, not only on hover.
Do not put links or buttons inside it.
Let Escape close it.

month-calendar.what: A calendar page showing a whole month as a grid of days, with the events that fall on each day.
uses: Planning bookings, rotas and deadlines across weeks.
Seeing which days are busy or free.
Choosing dates for events.
avoid: Exact times in one or two days: use a day or week view.
Many events per day: use an agenda list.
practices: Show today clearly.
Limit events per day and add a '+N more' link.
Start the week on the day users expect.
Make each day open its detail.

week-view.what: A calendar view with seven day columns on an hour grid, so each event shows its length and time of day.
uses: Scheduling meetings, shifts or appointments in a week.
Spotting clashes between events.
Planning around work hours.
avoid: Overview of a whole month: use a month view.
Small screens: use a day or agenda view.
practices: Show a line for the current time.
Place overlapping events side by side.
Include an all-day row.
Scroll to the start of the working day.

day-view.what: A calendar view of one day on an hour grid, with room to show full event details.
uses: Phones and narrow screens.
A person's or a room's busy day.
Days with many events.
avoid: Planning across several days: use a week or multi-day view.
A simple list of what is next: use an agenda.
practices: Make events large enough to tap.
Show title, time and place for each event.
Let people change day easily.
Show the current time.

agenda-view.what: A list of upcoming events grouped by day, with times and details, instead of a grid.
uses: Phones and small screens.
A 'what is next' panel.
A screen reader friendly or printable calendar.
avoid: Seeing gaps in a schedule: use a grid view.
Dragging events to new times: use a grid view.
practices: Group events under clear date headings.
Skip days with nothing planned.
Show time and place for each event.
Show a friendly message when nothing is planned.

year-view.what: A calendar showing all twelve months at once, with days that have events marked.
uses: Planning holidays and annual schedules.
Picking dates far ahead.
Seeing the pattern of a whole year.
avoid: Details of a single day: use a month or day view.
Many events per day: use a list.
practices: Mark days with events by a dot, not only colour.
Highlight today.
Make every day open its detail.
Keep month labels clear and consistent.

multi-day-view.what: A calendar view showing a few days side by side on an hour grid, such as today and the next two days.
uses: Tablets and side panels.
A short look ahead at upcoming days.
Teams planning across a few days.
avoid: A full week: use a week view.
One busy day: use a day view.
practices: Pick a number of days that fits the width.
Show times down one side.
Show the current time.
Let people move forward and back.

calendar-toolbar.what: The control bar above a calendar, used to move between periods, switch views and add events.
uses: Moving to the previous or next period.
Switching between day, week and month.
Starting a new event.
avoid: Page-level navigation: use a site menu.
Filtering which calendars show: use a legend.
practices: Keep it in the same place on every view.
Show the period title clearly.
Give a Today button to get back quickly.
Put the create button last.

mini-calendar-sidebar.what: A side panel next to a main calendar with a small month for jumping to a date, plus options such as a create button and calendar list.
uses: Jumping to a date far from today.
Calendars with several sources to filter.
Full calendar pages on desktop.
avoid: Phone screens with little room: move it below or hide it.
Simple calendars with one source.
practices: Match the selected day to the main view.
Mark days that have events.
Keep the create button at the top.
Move the panel below the calendar on small screens.

calendar-legend.what: A list of the calendars or event types on view, each with its colour, that lets people show or hide them.
uses: Calendars that mix events from several sources.
Letting people focus on what matters now.
Explaining what each colour means.
avoid: A single calendar with one colour: no key is needed.
Filters with many options: use a filter panel.
practices: Show each name beside its colour.
Never use colour as the only clue.
Use checkboxes to show or hide.
Keep the list short.

live-example.what: A panel that shows a working example of a piece of interface next to the code that makes it.
uses: Design-system and component documentation.
Style guides and tutorials.
Showing how an API or widget behaves.
avoid: Long code files: link to the source instead.
Screenshots of static content: use an image.
practices: Make sure the preview and code match.
Show the preview first, code second.
Let people copy the code easily.
Keep each example small and focused.

code-block.what: A formatted area that shows lines of code or commands in an even-width font, usually with a copy button.
uses: Documentation with commands and examples.
Showing settings or configuration.
Sharing API keys or tokens that people copy.
avoid: A single word or short name in a sentence: use inline code.
Long files: link to the source.
practices: Offer a Copy button and confirm it worked.
Name the language.
Keep samples short and runnable.
Scroll sideways instead of wrapping lines.

docs-nav-tree.what: A side menu for documentation that groups pages into sections and often has a search box to find a page quickly.
uses: Documentation sites with many pages.
Help centres.
Design-system guides.
avoid: Sites with only a few pages: use a simple menu.
Main product navigation: use a site menu.
practices: Group pages into clear sections.
Highlight the current page.
Let people filter by name.
Keep section names short.

email-frame.what: The standard layout wrapped around an automatic email, with a header, message, one main button and a footer.
uses: Welcome and sign-up emails.
Password reset messages.
Alerts and report notifications.
avoid: Marketing newsletters with many sections: use an email tool.
Long documents: link to a web page.
practices: Keep the width around 600 pixels or less.
Offer one clear action and print its link too.
Always include a plain-text version.
Say the event in the subject line.
